“A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step". This famous saying attributed to Lao Tzu, founder of Taoism and author of the Tao Te Ching, encapsulates my current understanding of 21st Century Leadership. For me leadership is a process that is dynamic and ever unfolding; a journey versus a destination; with unexpected (and expected) twists and turns, ups and downs, lefts and rights, advances, retreats, and going around in circles. This essay is an evidence-based approach to contemporary leadership that I synthesized through a recent course.   

Comparing the 21st vs. the 20th century leader: an overall perspective​ 

Listed below are some points that 21st century leaders need to be cognizant of; points that were neither widely acknowledged nor considered important enough, in the previous century.   

·Be open-minded and open-hearted; be authentically generous in giving and receiving feedback.

·Be deliberate in building inclusive and diverse teams.

·Enhance gender diversity through design vs default; as this century progresses, perhaps transcending gender itself may become a leadership aspiration?

·Nurture like-minded individuals in your teams; help them articulate and achieve their personal and professional goals because in their success is your success.

·Elicit viewpoints from people who are unlike-minded or contrarian, but if those people are obnoxious, disrespectful, and narcissistic (within the garb of contrarianism), then ignore their viewpoints.

·Be mission/vision/purpose-driven; work towards something that is much bigger than yourself that shall help you contribute to the 'music of the universe'. 

·Do not encourage incentivization models that merely focus on short-term gratifications, to the detriment of the individual's growth and detracts from organizational long-term vision/strategy.

·Encourage critical, creative, innovative, and entrepreneurial thinking in your teams. Offer them safe spaces for ideation or for venting if/when needed; spaces that are non-judgmental and non-hierarchical.

·Be data-driven - however, recall that data is not necessarily knowledge nor wisdom. In striving for data, do not forget to listen to people - empathize with them and their needs. Recall that technology/data can be your friend, but it is simply a means to an end; it should not end up controlling you - the leader - nor your subordinates/teams.

· Accountability, transparency, and organizational ethical frameworks are key. Impartial internal and external audits can ensure higher work quality and staff satisfaction. ​

Taking on a new leadership role, assessing your team, and openly communicating with it

 Before taking on a new leadership role, consider asking several of the following questions, with the caveat that you may not get all the answers. The answers that you do get would not only help you make a decision, but also to assess your new team and how to remain transparent with it.

·What will be my governance structure, organogram, or reporting line?

·To achieve my goals, would I be allowed to function autonomously through adequate resources and calculated risk taking?

·What are the organizational core values (or guiding principles); but more than that, is the prevalent culture close to or far from those putative values?

·Does the organization believe that I have the expertise or skillset for the new leadership role, what are its expectations of me, and how will my success be gauged?

·Who will be my team and who are the enablers and disablers within that team?

·What are the lines of organizational communication, internal as well as external, and how clear and transparent are they?

Leadership perspective on collaborating, inspiring and governing

There are some excellent concepts of creative workplaces' collaboration, two of which I describe here. David Kelley's approach through IDEO1 is reminiscent of human-centered design thinking emphasizing your team's crazy/wild ideas with unclear or unexpected outcomes (for complex 'messy' problems) - a strategy likely to work for mavericks (aka risk-takers). The Mass Animation2 approach of crowdsourcing independent creativity within a framework is also quite intriguing; given the pre-determined scope vis-a-vis outcome, the ability of collaborative group work through cooperation creates its own leadership challenges and opportunities. Personally, as a leader, I would like to try out and contextualize IDEO's approach for my own team of ideators, innovators, and entrepreneurs. Autonomy, mastery, and purpose can be strongly motivational for people in 21st century organizations. Respecting people and their ideas, not judging those ideas, and not always pushing for that single best idea amongst a lot of ideas, are additional points to consider. With respect to effective governance impacting organizational transformation, revising the board of governors towards a leaner and more flexible and agile group will ensure that it has more skin in the game.

Managing talented people through diversity, inclusion and innovation

The 'dandelion principle' 3 for managing talent inspires inclusion and diversity at the workplace, and although it may require a paradigm shift, it is quite worth it for the 21st-century. Given the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, the fractures and faults of organizations and their inherent processes have become all the more obvious, hence utilizing the dandelion metaphor to manage talent in these unprecedented times makes even more sense. We need places and spaces (real and virtual) that are inclusive, equitable, and respectful of people who are differently abled. Recognizing so will help us manage people, keeping their authenticities in mind - and we will be less likely to force them to conform to traditionally set ritualistic attitudes and systems. Ultimately, I hope that we move closer to workplaces that celebrate diversity in everything and everyone, and that will become the sine qua non for impactful innovation, creativity and, entrepreneurship for 21st-century organizations globally with transgenerational workforces. With diversely talented people, innovation would become an easier call to action because of creative freedom through adequate spaces (actual and virtual), with appropriate access to capital, time, and expertise.

Leading in crisis, execution of strategy, and the role of organizational culture

'Never waste a good crisis' is a very insightful statement for a leader, because that is his/her opportunity to lead by example, walk the talk, and be a real team player. The leader can loop in the most trustworthy people to engage with the board members through one-to-one conversations to get them to agree to her crisis mode strategy. In tandem recalling further that no matter how bad things are, they will get worse would help her keep on her toes vis-a-vis ongoing risk mitigation and damage control. No matter how brilliant the strategy may be, the proof of the pudding lies in execution. In other words, weak execution eats great strategy for breakfast. How not to lead in a crisis was evident from the lessons learnt from the financial crisis of 2008, in which there were several failures of leadership4. First and foremost it seemed like the Wall Street CEOs and other high-powered bankers/investors/executives/politicians were more driven by greed, self-interest, egos, etc. They demonstrated characteristics that were reminiscent of the transactional and great man theories of leadership. There was no higher purpose; they lacked a vision; other than instant gratification, the huge amounts of bonuses that those folks collected, while millions of individuals across the globe suffered. Moving away from the transactional leadership theory and towards ethical and transformational styles was the take home for me.

With regards to the 'role of culture' all companies are not alike, but the dilemma of cultural change management is likely the same. A non-hierarchical approach that is less dependent on approval seeking vs. quick prototyping, experimenting, and fast failing/pivoting, will also be indicative of a paradigm shift in culture: in other words, the 'just do it and ask for forgiveness later' approach. Communication (both upward and downward) is key and with both simple and complex tools of IT/tech, this may be achieved relatively easily. For a leader who is an outsider, culture can be beneficial by allowing agile innovative practices. The inbred leader is unlikely to even consider the need for change, or instituting that sense of urgency, since he/she may become more complacent because of biases. In the final analysis, culture can be both a challenge and an opportunity for transformation.

The 21st century leader's public- vs. private-life dilemma

Since there is a thin line dividing personal/private from professional/public, whatever happens in one domain will likely impact the other. A leader's private behavior is very relevant to his/her leadership abilities and performance. One can argue that a leader's private life is of no one's concern but his, and I agree with that. But as we have observed in real life such a clear distinction between public life-private life does not really exist past a certain point, especially for high profile leaders. Our expectations of our leaders in their so-called private matters should be held to a very high moral/ethical ground; as high if not higher than that of their public/professional matters. Having said that, we also need to be cognizant of the famous proverb 'to err is human to forgive divine'. While keeping that in mind, we could practice compassion by giving the leader a chance to rectify his/her mistake(s). Over time, as we grow as human beings, I think the realization that our moral compass or moral obligation needs to be more inwards directed rather than outwardly manifested, will help us become better leaders of our own lives.

Conclusion

Given the chaotic 21st century I believe leadership needs to be flexible and adaptive to the situation at hand. I find transformational leadership most meaningful from the creativity and innovation perspective; the kind of openness for trying new things, accepting failure as part of the innovation process, facilitating your team members' self-actualization, and so on, can be a powerful approach while in the 'business as usual' mode. Going past leadership theory, the role of experiential learning and having intimate knowledge of organizational culture in enhancing performance cannot be ignored. Next time you find yourself in a difficult leadership dilemma, consider concocting your personal leadership approach, albeit through an evidence base while monitoring outcomes. That may help you pivot to the leadership style that is most appropriate for the situation you find yourself in.

Blog Detail:
The huge poster at the mall grabs my attention. There's a mom in her kitchen with her kids around her. The children are creating a supreme mess in the kitchen (in the said poster), as expected, but mom is peaceful - levitating in a yoga-like posture, seemingly practicing mindfulness meditation, hence the caption 'Breathe Mama, Breathe!' is quite appropriate, I think.     

Happy Mother's Day it says at the bottom of the poster, albeit in small print. That's what it's likely advocating for. It is, after all, one of the busiest 'C' days per my lexicon, i.e. commercialistic/capitalistic/consumeristic, when people shop till they drop at all kinds of sales events at malls. Perhaps some of what they purchase is for their moms.  

I'm also there, but unlike most, I believe I'm actually there shopping for my Ma. She has given me a list of what to obtain for her kitchen in Karachi. I'm in Houston for a work-related trip and on that last day of my visit there, the mandatory stop at a mall – any mall – is needed to pick up Ma's stuff. That it happens to be around Mother's Day is an intriguing coincidence. Ma has asked me for a specific kind of lemon squeezer from Bed, Bath & Beyond. I'm in a time crunch as I have to be at the airport in an hour. So, I decide to pick up any lemon squeezer that I can find in that mall – the adjoining Target comes to my rescue, and I do the needful.

Armed with a few more (presumably) random things for Ma that I pick up from the mall, I head out to the airport.

After checking in and screening I barely have enough time to make my way to the gate and board the flight.

I get to my seat and I curse the travel agent for assigning me to the middle of a row of three seats. The thought of a ten-hour flight squeezed between two passengers is far from pleasant. Someday perhaps work travel will be escalated to business class and such space restrictions will go away? 

I put on my seatbelt and try to make myself as comfortable as I can. I switch my cell phone to plane mode, put on my headphones to listen to my playlist, and then I pull out my book that I'm really excited to read during the flight. The book is titled 'Homo Deus – a brief history of tomorrow' by Noah Yuval Harari. If you haven't read it then give it a shot. It's worth your read.   

I must have read no more than a few lines when I feel a tap on my left shoulder.

It's a really old lady in the more desirable window seat next to mine trying to get my attention.  

“Kiya parh rahay ho?" (What are you reading?)

My excitement to read about humanity's future fizzles out promptly and I put the book aside. I have a premonition that the interaction that shall ensue over the course of the flight will not be a brief one. I fleetingly recall the encounter with Ernie several years back on a flight from New York. He was a septuagenarian with whom I had struck a fascinating discourse while up in the air, albeit hesitatingly as I don't belong to the small talk brigade. This time it is happening with an even older person - very likely a nonagenarian I think.  

Her head is covered by a large chador that she's tightly wrapped around herself because it's quite cold in there. Her spectacles are perched on the tip of her nose; they have really thick lenses that magnify her eyes manifold. She's clutching a plastic bag. History really seems to be repeating itself. Ernie too had been clutching a plastic bag in his lap all those years ago. Perhaps this is the norm for the very elderly in long-distance flights – they hold on to plastic bags for dear life.

“Kitab mein kiya hai?" (What's in the book?) The old lady asks again.

Unsure how to explain complex concepts of artificial intelligence and virtual reality and their impact on humanity's evolution in Urdu - or Hindi as I'm still unsure whether she's from India or Pakistan - I keep the answer simple and noncommittal.

“Ma ji, science kay baray mein hai" (Mother, it's about science)

Calling her mother is quite inadvertent and spontaneous. In fact, 'Ma ji' is even more of an endearment than just 'Ma' as the former reverently addresses an elderly mother or mother-like lady. Hence it feels appropriate, given her age and South Asian lineage.

By that time boarding is complete and the announcement for seat belts to be secured and seat backs to be upright is ongoing.

I glance at Ma ji. She looks back at me and then down at her unfastened seat belt. She unsuccessfully tries to belt herself into her seat. I note the characteristic hands of the elderly – frail fingers bent out of shape because of arthiritis.

I ask if I can fasten her seatbelt for her. She mumbles something so without waiting for a coherent answer I do it for her while explaining what I am doing and apologizing too as I'm uncomfortable encroaching on her space.

Once settled and belted into her seat, she opens the plastic bag and reveals to me her cache of chocolates within - Snickers, Mars, and Bounty. She takes a bite of a Mars bar and then offers me some. I politely decline. I wonder if she's diabetic. I'm like that; the itinerant doctor in me closely observes the young and old to generate differential diagnoses (disease possibilities, in other words) all the time. Thus far I've given Ma ji two potential diagnoses: arthritis and diabetes. Along with that and the backdrop of extreme elderliness, she's likely high risk to have an event in flight. A cardiac event, to be precise – heart attack or such. My mind gets even more creative and imaginative: what if she does have an event and I respond to the overhead call 'is there any doctor on board to attend to a medical emergency?' I've responded to two mid-flight emergencies before. Dealing with those was fine as I happen to be a pediatric emergency physician. But will I be able to do anything useful for Ma ji given the other end of the age spectrum?

“Tera Naam?" (Your name?) she asks curtly, and that brings me out of my reverie.      

“Asad" I respond, realizing once again the inevitability of further conversation.

“Ajay?"

“No…no…Asad". I respond louder.

“Ajay, mein Houston apnay baray larkay kay saath thi. Ab India wapas ja rahin hoon" [Ajay, I was with my older son in Houston. Now I'm returning to India]

I don't correct her anymore. I start enjoying the interaction. Might as well.

I expect a high likelihood of 'where are you from / where are you going / what do you do' type flight-like interrogation, but it seems like Ma Ji is more interested in venting.  

 “Meray teen larkay hain, koi beti nahin. Lekin meray do betay jo India mein hain who mujhe der tak nahin rakhtay". [I have three sons, no daughter. But the two sons in India don't let me stay with them for long periods]   

Although Ma Ji goes on to describe her eldest son's job in Houston, I'm unable to grasp exactly what it is that he does. The closest I can get to is that he's either in construction or truck driving, perhaps both based on her description. She also gives ample coverage to her 'gori' (white / Caucasian, I assume) daughter-in-law. Ma ji sounds a bit disapproving talking about her daughter-in-law: a primary school teacher, unable to spend time tending to her sick mother-in-law, nor doting enough for her hubby and kids.  

I just nod my head a lot and that seems sufficient enough for her to continue her monologue. No questions are asked, nor comments elicited, as her narrative unfolds and that is fine by me.     

It's been almost two hours into the flight now and I'm pleasantly surprised that my fellow traveler has managed to keep me quite entertained thus far.

By that time the flight attendants are busy serving dinner and beverages.

“Will you have the chicken or beef?" The attendant asks Ma ji. 

“Halal?" is her curt response-cum-question.

“Meat is not kosher. Shall I get you the vegetable pasta, instead?"

“Na!" she responds with an edge in her tone. Monosyllabic answers I also note. Likely because her English-speaking skills aren't up to mark, although her comprehension is good?   

However, I'm intrigued as to why she's unable to comprehend my very Muslim name – in fact, she creates a Hindu version of it – and yet she's adamant about halal food. Is she Hindu or Muslim? I'm curious but too polite to ask. Although truth be told, does it even matter what faith she subscribes to?

There's silence over the next hour or so as I consume the chicken entre that I've selected, while she periodically partakes of candy from her plastic bag.   

Once I'm done with my meal and everything's cleared up, I'm recharged enough to continue the conversation, if it even can be called so. When I look over I realize she's nodded off and is snoring. Thus, obstructive sleep apnea also enters my list of differentials.    

Over the next few hours I also try to catch some sleep, but as is always the case during long-distance travel, a meaningful nap eludes me. I try watching a movie or two from the in-flight entertainment list, but I'm quite unsuccessful there too. Between the alternating attempt to sleep and focus on a movie, I likely fall asleep and even dream because the next thing I remember is being woken up by Ma ji.     ​

“Bathroom jana hai" (I need to go to the bathroom) She says.

I let her pass. She returns after what seems like an eternity as I've dozed off again.

Once she's resettled in her seat, she goes back to her chocolates and offers me one. This time I don't refuse and accept a Bounty bar.  

And before I realize it, she's resumed her monologue.

What I piece together is that she gets bounced back and forth between her sons in India and the US. Once she's revealed quite a bit of her fragmented life in India and the US, she presents a detailed assessment of the many more pros of living in the East versus the West. She doesn't have a permanent home of her own anymore. Her husband passed away decades ago. She disapproves of the peripatetic turn that her life has taken since she's been widowed.     

Although she comes across as fiercely independent, I realize how fragile she really is. Her façade of 'being able to do it all still' falls by the wayside by a bit of cajoling on my part. She succumbs quite easily to my attempts to make her flight more comfortable when I ask her if she would like some fruit, water, chai, etc. (all halal).

And in such a manner the rest of the flight is completed. 

Once the airplane lands and I walk down the aisle towards the exit, I turn back to get one last look at Ma ji; she appears quite forlorn and lost. I wave to her, but she does not respond. She looks through me as if she's already forgotten. I feel pensive leaving her behind, still seated, but the flight attendant reassures me on my way out that the old lady will be taken care of; a helper is on his way with a wheelchair.

I then let go of her and think of my Ma instead. I wonder if some stranger in a parallel universe is assisting Ma either at an airport or in flight to ease her journey?

I hope so…​

Blog Detail:
​Given the recent surge in 'TOP 10 ​​​everything under the sun​' lists, I too felt like coming up with a list of 10 items. 'Top 10 parenting skills' and 'Top 10 dog names' came to mind, as I had previously written about parenting and keeping a dog, albeit in separate articles.
However, as soon as I thought of those topics, my mind discarded them as something else ​intrigued me more. Closer to the end of the year, perhaps as a new year's resolution, the ​question that I pondered upon was: is there any purpose to life, and if so, what might it be?

Based on that, a list of 10 things that I believed in came to mind because, you see, prior to figuring out your life's purpose, you must believe that there can be such a thing as life's purpose.


Thus, here I share my top 10 beliefs, in no particular order:

1.       I need to love myself 

For that I first need to be myself and then like myself. I must stop being harsh on or judgmental about myself or others. And I must stop blaming myself, or others for my life's perceived mess.

2.      I need not simply be who I am, but who I am meant to be

For that I need to do away with all my 'baggage': cultural, religious, societal, capitalistic, and consumerist notions about pretty much everything. In order to get to my core or essence, 'stripped of everything, who am I really?' is the question that needs to be addressed.

3.      I need to let my mind be still

​​Only then will I be able to reflect on my life and where it is headed. During this reprieve I exercise regularly, eat healthy, drink lots of fluids; I rest my mind frequently; I pause to look at flowers, trees, squirrels, clouds, the sun, stars… perhaps easier said than done, but I make a conscious effort. It reminds me of my insignificance. Yet, when I am ready for 'change', I can look upon mountains and feel strong enough to move them as well.

4.      I need to be happy

Contrary to popular belief, the pursuit of happiness is not overrated. Therefore, I seek out what makes me happy and then pursue it, irrespective of fears of failure, rejection, or regret. Even when faced with challenges, I remain happy and I accept and learn to deal with them because they help me grow.

5.      I need to acknowledge my darkness 

And that it is there for a reason. Light would not be light if it were not for darkness, and vice versa. Opposites make up the whole. If I cannot entirely let go of the dark side, then I need to control it, versus the other way around.


6.      I need to be one with nature and people

I can truly love nature unconditionally, and she loves me back in a similar manner. And be one not just with 'my people', but people of all kinds, nationalities, cultures, religions, genders (or lack thereof), and ages. I can only do this once I stop being judgmental and superior.

7.       I need to stop fearing life and death

I need to love life. Recall that life is a gift, perhaps the greatest gift of all, hence, I must not wait for it to be taken away from me. So I live life, love life, live love and love love​– all in the here and now. That moment will either create my heaven or it will create my hell. But I can choose what I need from that moment. Living in the moment is 'what is', so why to worry about 'what if'. And that is how I stop fearing death.

8.      I need to attract positive with positive

That is one way to become the flow. I need to be like water: a positive life force as well as a positive flow. Water does not resist, and it will not be resisted by hurdles – it simply flows around or through road-blocks. But then water can be destructive too. Therefore, too much positivity is also not good as that can sap and zap me as well as those around me.

9.      I need to distinguish between true passion, an escape, and 'just fun' activities

Because my purpose or calling in life is likely tied into my passion. For instance, reading books, although a fun time-pass, might be a temporary escape from my daily reality. But it's not a passion. Writing might become a passion, but it does not pay the bills. So, finding a passion that I can tie into my daily routine at the workplace might make me achieve or reach a 'career high'.

10.   I need to find a teacher

Once I find a teacher or two, I stick to him, her, or it, as long as the need be. Only I can know who my teacher is. In my journeying, I might come across books (as teachers), either recommended by someone, or I might just stumble upon them myself. If I approach the 'right' books (poetry or prose) in a certain way, then I can get a lot of understanding of life and love. And I get signs or indication of my progress towards a purpose. But that process is hard and long. I must be patient, and I must not force reading upon myself, because that will do zilch. The best kind of learning is experiential – I learn from my own experiences, trial, and error initially, but then with increasing accuracy. My most sustainable teacher is myself and my core beliefs that have been stripped of conditioning. My best teachers are life and love.

Post-script: The author acknowledges that 'Top 10 needs' or perhaps '10 things to strive for' might have also been appropriate titles too for this essay, although that would have lacked creativity. He also acknowledges that this list of 10 beliefs has helped him move closer to his life's purpose.

‘Tabeer’ is an Urdu word that means ‘interpretation’ or ‘meaning,’ often used in the context of dreams. 

As we embarked on the Tabeer initiative, a landmark program crafted to mold the next generation of leaders of the Institute of Business Administration (IBA) through the core values of Compassion, Communication, and Creative Leadership, I found myself deeply immersed in a dream like journey that was as much a discovery for myself as it was for the participants. It occurred to me that Tabeer was powerfully symbolic: the program's aim was to unlock or interpret the potential, meaning, and purpose in future leaders, guiding them to a deeper understanding of their capabilities, values, and the impact they can have through leadership.

This initiative, a joint venture between IBA and Synapse, stands as a testament to the collaborative spirit and visionary zeal of individuals who believe in the transformative power of leadership. Dr. Ayesha Mian - formerly an Associate Professor and Chair of Psychiatry at Aga Khan University (AKU) -  as the Founder and CEO of Synapse Pakistan Neuroscience Institute, and her profound expertise in behavioral science, played a pivotal role in this endeavor. Her insights into the neuroscience of leadership dynamics have been instrumental in setting a solid foundation for the program. With her intrepid team members, the primary purpose of this initiative has been to promote tolerance, celebrate opposing viewpoints, upend the status quo, and ultimately change the way we view differences. 

My own journey, as a Professor and past Chair of the Department of Emergency Medicine and Director of the Critical Creative Innovative Thinking (CCIT) Forum at AKU, has always been about exploring the intersections of healthcare innovation and leadership. With our book ‘Medjack’ and my active engagement in innovation and business incubation, I aimed to offer IBA participants a practical model to understand and harness the power of failure in cultivating forward-thinking solutions. My article in Dawn on celebrating failure was an attempt to articulate a nuanced perspective on failure, not just as an inevitable part of the innovation journey but as a milestone worth celebrating.

The richness of the Tabeer initiative was significantly enhanced by the contributions of Unjela Kaleem, Principal of International Development and Humanitarian Assistance at Miyamoto International. As the keynote speaker, Unjela brought a profound depth of knowledge in storytelling and strategic communications, underscoring the importance of these skills in effective leadership. By placing a strong emphasis on Compassion, Communication, and Creative Leadership, and adopting a progressive stance on failure, we can prepare our students for leadership paths that not only embrace but celebrate failures as essential to personal and professional growth.

I had the privilege and honour of being a panelist at The Global Digital Health Summit 2024, hosted by The Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. This is a platform for experts to delve into the transformative potential of digital health.

I had the opportunity to share insights from a low-income setting, alongside esteemed colleagues. The session, moderated by Asma Rayani and Hrishikesh Sathyamoorthy, featured discussions led by Dr. Asad Latif on digital technology's impact on patient safety, Dr. Chris Fore on telehealth in behavioural healthcare, and Dr. Surjit Nundy on the empowerment of patients through digital health.

Representing the Department of Emergency Medicine and the Critical Creative Innovative Thinking (CCIT) Forum at Aga Khan University in Pakistan, I focused on illustrating how digital health fosters creative solutions to the complex challenges faced by low-resource emergency departments. These are my deeper reflections based on the questions asked during the discussion. 

Q1. As the director of the CCIT forum, how do you foster a culture of creativity and innovation among healthcare professionals? Could you provide examples of low-cost, high-impact innovations developed under your leadership?

I cultivated a culture of creativity and innovation by embracing three core characteristics. First, the non-hierarchical approach that ensured individuals from various fields felt empowered to contribute equally to the innovation process. In our hackathons, medical students collaborate with engineers and designers to develop solutions for pressing healthcare challenges. 

Second, the cross-disciplinary collaboration. This approach allows us to address healthcare challenges from multiple angles and develop innovative solutions that consider various aspects of patient care. In a recent project, nurses collaborated with software developers to design a mobile application for patient monitoring in intensive care units, resulting in improved efficiency and patient outcomes.  

And thirdly, the intergenerational knowledge exchange. This approach fosters mentorship and collaboration between seasoned professionals and emerging talents. Experienced clinicians mentor medical students and junior faculty members, sharing insights and guiding them through the innovation process. 

Our flagship hackathons exemplify the essence of CCIT, bringing together interdisciplinary teams to tackle pressing healthcare challenges. One of our hackathons focused on improving patient triage in emergency departments, resulting in the development of a low-cost, high-impact solution that streamlined the triaging process.

Q2. In your view what are the most promising digital health technologies for improving patient outcomes in emergency departments, especially in resource-constrained environments?

Telemedicine facilitates timely and accessible healthcare services extending reach to remote areas, and mobile health apps that engage patients in self-management. Additionally, implementing health information systems (HIS/EHR) can digitize and streamline documentation processes ensuring continuity of care in resource-constrained environments. 

Moreover, remote patient monitoring technologies enable continuous monitoring of patient’s vital signs outside traditional healthcare settings. By leveraging wearable devices and mobile apps, emergency departments can remotely monitor high-risk patients and intervene proactively to prevent complications. While health analytics, powered by artificial intelligence and machine learning, can identify high-risk patients through triaging, predicting severity and outcomes.  

However, it is important to note that successful implementation of the above technologies in resource-constrained environments requires addressing challenges such as limited infrastructure and healthcare professionals training. A holistic approach emphasizing capacity building, stakeholder engagement, and sustainable financing is essential for realizing the full potential. 

Q3. Could you discuss the intersection between healthcare, entrepreneurship, and innovation, particularly in the context of developing sustainable solutions in low-resource settings?

Healthcare needs serve as the foundation for entrepreneurship and innovation. Contextual entrepreneurship is crucial in translating innovative ideas into scalable ventures, fostering innovation cultures, and driving meaningful change through collaborations. The intersection of healthcare, entrepreneurship, and innovation is pivotal, particularly where the concept of ‘jugaar’ is essential. Frugal innovation, emphasizing affordability and scalability, holds promise by leveraging resourcefulness and ingenuity for impactful solutions.

Nevertheless, sustainable solutions require a comprehensive understanding of socio-cultural, economic, and political contexts addressing systemic barriers to unlock the full potential of digital health technologies for improved health outcomes and sustainable development goals.

Q4. As an educator, how do you prepare the next generation of emergency medicine professionals to integrate digital health tools into their practice?

Curriculum integration ensures that digital health concepts are incorporated into residency and fellowship programmes. Interdisciplinary collaborations expose students to diverse perspectives and skills, while hands-on training and clinical rotations develop practical skills and provide real world experience. Innovation and digital health fellowships offer specialized training, while continuing education maintains professionalism as ethical and legal considerations are emphasized. By integrating digital health education and embracing a multidisciplinary approach, educators prepare future professionals to deliver patient-centered care in the digital age.

Q5. Can you share insights into your quality initiatives in paediatric emergency care? How do these initiatives address the unique challenges of emergency medicine for children?

Specialized training equips healthcare professionals with skills in paediatric resuscitation, trauma management, and critical care. Guidelines ensure standardized approaches to assessment, triage, and treatment, including dosing calculations for medications and age-appropriate techniques.

Paediatric-centric approaches encompass specialized equipment and child life specialists to provide emotional support and pain management. Child protection teams address the prevalence of child abuse and neglect in the community.

Integration of paediatric emergency medicine into broader health systems ensures continuity of care, while community education raises awareness about paediatric health issues, including preventive measures and timely access to emergency care.
Blog Title: Charting Our Digital Future: My Takeaways from the Global Digital Health Summit 2024

In the bustling streets of Karachi, Pakistan, where four schools buzzed with the energy of young minds eager to learn, lurked a challenge. It was a challenge that set us on an adventure into the world of vaccination and disease prevention. 

In this adventure, we embarked on a journey of discovery. Where colorful storybooks and animated videos, became heroes in the fight against diseases.

This journey began with a group of brave children, aged 8 to 12, who volunteered to be part of a special mission into the world of vaccination awareness, led by wise researchers.  

In 2015, a group of pioneers set out to spread awareness on road safety, armed with the Biloongra books that were developed by Dr. Asad I. Mian. They used pre and post test questionnaires on the same day, accompanied by a post-test 2 months later to assess the knowledge retention. The results of this study indicated a positive response. It emphasized that books with simple illustrations and engaging narratives captivate children's hearts and minds.

Fortunately, the magic didn't end there. Bookgroup, the masterminds behind these enchanting books, created an animated episode titled "Biloongra ki Shararat" (Biloongra’s Mischief). This grand adventure featured schools that embraced both the book and video. 

The researchers split the children into two groups: The first group, “Urdu Avengers,” dove into the pages of a traditional book with vibrant illustrations and words in Urdu. While the second group, “English Defenders,” embarked on a journey through the English animated video.  As the story unfolded, the children learned the magic of vaccines, how they prevent illness, and why timing of vaccination is key. Through the adventures of characters in the storybooks and videos, they discovered the importance of protecting newborns, how to respond to sports injuries, and how vaccines boost immunization. Tests were administered before and after their adventures to measure their knowledge about vaccinations. 

The children had not just learned; they had become champions of immunization. Analysis of the Urdu Avengers showed a statistically significant increase in understanding why they get sick. Similarly, substantial shifts were observed in their knowledge on when vaccines are administered, and strategies to protect newborns from paralysis. They also demonstrated outstanding shifts in recommendations for addressing a child's injury. 

Meanwhile, the English Defenders also showed significant change in perspectives. There was a statistically significant increase in understanding causes of illness, as well as in recommended actions when participants become sick. Furthermore, they demonstrated notable shifts in perceiving appropriate times for vaccine administration, and the safety with getting vaccinated. Their perspectives on measles prevention and managing sports-related injuries also changed. 

Conversely, understanding the protection of newborns from certain diseases displayed a notable reduction. Insights regarding advocating universal vaccination and the efficacy of games in enhancing memory showed relatively minor changes.

While the children showed remarkable improvement, there was a hint of forgetfulness. This observation highlighted the need for sustained efforts to maintain vaccine safety and immunization knowledge retention.  

All things said and done, we recognize the limitations of our journey – the absence of a control group, potential biases, and the need for longer-term assessments. Yet, armed with our findings, we pave the way for future adventures, where innovative approaches to vaccination education shape a healthier, brighter world.

In the battle against under-immunization, education is our greatest weapon. By creating bilingual pictorial storybooks and animated videos, we can empower children to understand the importance of vaccinations. Large-scale trials can evaluate the effectiveness of the intervention and assess which group gains more. There is potential to replicate similar models as a global health imperative.
Blog Title: Urdu Avengers and English Defenders out on an Adventure
Summary: Biloongra-based Storytelling to Improve Vaccine Literacy Amongst School Children in Karachi

Kazungu , a community health extension worker (CHEW) in Kilifi County, has witnessed firsthand the struggles pregnant women in his community face when trying to access ultrasound services. The nearest health facilities that provided ultrasound were often too far away, and procedure was too expensive. As a result, many pregnant women would have to travel long distances and pay exorbitant fees in order to access the service, and they would occasionally be turned away due to overwhelmed facilities. These barriers discouraged women from having the necessary scans, leading to missed opportunities for early intervention.

Asha (not her real name), a mother from Kinarani Dispensary, Kilifi, represents countless others who have faced similar challenges. Despite knowing the benefits of ultrasound scans, she was unable to afford the service at the local healthcare facility. Tragically, Asha lost one of her twins during childbirth, which could have been prevented if she had been referred sooner.

In maternal healthcare, access to ultrasound can determine pregnancy outcomes. The World Health Organization recommends at least one ultrasound scan before 24 weeks of pregnancy for assessing viability, gestational age, and early detection of foetal and pregnancy problems, enabling early referral of at-risk pregnancies. However, many women in resource-limited areas struggle to access these services due to cost and availability issues.

To address this problem, Aga Khan University’s Centre of Excellence in Women and Child Health, East Africa, has collaborated with the Philips Foundation, Philips and the Kilifi County Government to increase access to ultrasound services at the primary healthcare level, making them accessible and affordable. Over 5000 pregnant women in Kilifi have received free ultrasounds as a result of this long-term collaboration, bringing us closer to bridging the maternal healthcare gap.

Salma, a dedicated nurse at Dida Dispensary in Ganze sub-county, Kilifi, benefited from this collaboration during her third pregnancy. When she experienced excessive pain, she sought reassurance through an ultrasound scan at one of the beneficiary sites, Mariakani sub-county hospital, which revealed that she was expecting twins. This early detection allowed her to adjust her pregnancy care accordingly.

Salma highlights the significance of the free ultrasound, offered through this collaboration, to her pregnancy journey. “In my previous pregnancies, I could only afford one ultrasound scan. This time, I had access to a second scan because the service was free,” she says. A follow-up scan at six months made a critical revelation that the babies were in breech position enabling her to plan for a safer delivery process. Eventually, her journey ended in the joyful arrival of two healthy babies.

Salma’s experience stands as a testament to the transformative impact of accessible ultrasound services in maternal healthcare. “When the 2016 WHO guidelines came to effect, we thought it would be hard to implement them fully. Thanks to Aga Khan University, supported by Philips, it is now becoming a reality,” says Kenneth Miriti, Kilifi County’s Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) coordinator. “We are seeing a lot of change in indicators from the two sub counties, referrals are being made early due to early detections by nurses-midwives trained through this project.”

And it doesn’t end there. Using artificial intelligence (AI), the partners introduced an AI-enabled obstetrics study aimed at making ultrasound scans more accessible and affordable to women in Kilifi and elsewhere. AI-driven ultrasound scans can help to maintain high-quality standards in maternal care while also providing a cost-effective option. 

We can create a safer and more equitable environment for women by increasing access to point-of-care ultrasound services and using the power of digital technology, ultimately contributing to improved maternal and child health outcomes.

Disclaimer: For privacy reasons, some names in this story have been changed to protect the identities of the individuals involved.
Blog Title: Breaking barriers: Advancing maternal healthcare through accessible ultrasound services

As several countries across the globe approach a significant election year, a fresh look at disinformation and misinformation is crucial. Last time, I advocated for enhancing media and information literacy as a countermeasure to the spread of falsehoods. I argued that merely criminalizing the dissemination of fake news was insufficient; equipping the public with skills to verify information was equally essential. Since then, I’ve engaged in numerous initiatives aimed at bolstering fact-checking and verification among various groups.

Now, with elections stirring up fervour across the globe—particularly in Africa, where countries like Nigeria, Senegal, South Africa, and Rwanda have recently held elections and Ghana is preparing for its December polls—the issue of disinformation becomes even more pressing. Election seasons often become fertile ground for misinformation campaigns, aimed at swaying voters through deepfakes, false narratives, and misleading information.

The World Economic Forum’s Global Risks Report 2024 highlights that misinformation and disinformation are anticipated to be among the greatest global threats in the coming years. The report warns that increasing mistrust in media and governments could exacerbate polarized views, potentially leading to civil unrest and conflict. This growing distrust is partly fuelled by the media's own shortcomings, including instances where it has been complicit in spreading misinformation.

A recent example from Ghana illustrates this troubling trend. Credible media outlets propagated false claims about a Guinness World Record, failing to apply the rigorous fact-checking that is fundamental to journalism. As Bill Kovach and Tom Rosenstiel emphasize in The Elements of Journalism, the discipline of verification is what differentiates journalism from entertainment or propaganda. The failure to adhere to these principles underscores a broader issue: the media’s role in perpetuating disinformation.

Disinformation is not a distant phenomenon but a pressing issue within Africa, including Ghana. There are organized entities dedicated to exploiting individuals' biases and naivety for financial gain through the dissemination of false information. During election cycles, misinformation often thrives due to inadequate information about electoral processes, which malicious actors exploit to spread deception that aligns with existing biases.

To combat this, election management bodies must ensure the timely and accurate dissemination of information to prevent the spread of falsehoods. However, the problem is compounded by the media’s often polarized nature, which can exacerbate divisions by presenting skewed narratives from politically motivated sources. This polarization is mirrored in the media’s tendency to focus on dichotomous perspectives rather than providing balanced, independent reporting.

As voters, it is crucial to navigate this landscape with a critical eye. The prevalence of disinformation means that it is easy to be ensnared in echo chambers that reinforce existing biases. To make informed electoral decisions, actively seek out diverse viewpoints rather than just those that align with your preconceptions. Avoid hastily accepting or sharing unverified information. Instead, challenge your biases and look for reliable sources that offer a well-rounded view of the issues at hand.

In addition, be judicious about sharing information. If you are unsure of its accuracy, refrain from passing it on. Mis/disinformation thrives on the rapid spread of unchecked content, so taking a moment to verify facts can help curb its influence.

In summary, as we navigate this election year, being proactive about information verification and remaining aware of the manipulative tactics used in disinformation campaigns will empower us to make more informed decisions and contribute to a healthier information environment.
Blog Title: Navigating Dis/Misinformation: A Media Consumer’s Guide
Summary: Learn to spot fake news and misinformation to make informed choices

Wandering through ARoS Aarhus Art Museum's five galleries, I stumbled upon a world of artistic wonders. From historical masterpieces to mind-bending installations, this Danish gem has ignited my creative spark.

ARoS is an art museum in Aarhus, Denmark. The museum was established in 1859 and is the oldest public art museum in Denmark outside Copenhagen. With five galleries and an entire floor dedicated to installation art, ARoS offers an important free space where it is possible to understand the past, explore the present and imagine the future in completely new ways.

While at ARoS, I learnt some tips and tricks that are relevant to my media and artistic practice.

When curating and producing an art exhibition, drawing inspiration from industry standard and practices is key to highlighting how African curators and producers can learn and adapt to showcase their art products in an immersive way:

  1. Embrace Immersive Experiences: The ARoS exhibition focuses on creating immersive environments that transport viewers into the artwork's world. African curators can consider:
    • Sound Design: Incorporate soundscapes or music that complement the artwork and enhance the visitor experience.
    • Scenography: Use lighting, props, and furniture to create distinct spaces within the exhibition that evoke different moods or themes.
  2. Engage with Technology: The ARoS exhibition leverages technology to create interactive experiences. African curators can explore:
    • Virtual Reality: Offer virtual tours or experiences that allow visitors to interact with artworks in new ways.
    • Augmented Reality: Overlay digital elements onto physical artworks, providing additional context or information.
  3. Curate Cross-Disciplinary Exhibitions: The ARoS exhibition blended art forms, creating unique and thought-provoking experiences. African curators can consider:
    • Collaborations: Partner with musicians, poets, or dancers to create performances or installations that complement the artwork.
    • Multisensory Experiences: Incorporate elements like scent, temperature or touch to engage visitors on a deeper level.
  4. Focus on Public Engagement: The ARoS exhibition prioritized public engagement through educational programs and workshops. African curators can:
    • Community Partnerships: Collaborate with local organizations to create exhibitions that reflect the community's interests and concerns.
    • Interactive Elements: Include hands-on activities or interactive displays that encourage visitor participation.
  5. Experiment with Exhibition Formats: The ARoS exhibition challenged traditional gallery settings. African curators can:
    • Pop-up Exhibitions: Utilize unconventional spaces like warehouses or rooftops to create temporary and unexpected experiences.
    • Site-Specific Installations: Create installations that are specifically designed for a particular location, taking advantage of its unique features. This was particularly interesting because I witnessed this at AKU's 40th anniversary exhibition 'A Transformative Vision'.
  6. Prioritize Accessibility: The ARoS exhibition strived to be accessible to all visitors. African curators can:
    • Translation and Interpretation: Provide translations and interpretation services for visitors who speak different languages.
    • Inclusive Design: Consider the needs of visitors with disabilities when designing the exhibition space and materials. Add chairs for people who need them. Add directional stickers on the floor to control human traffic within the gallery.
  7. Promote Local Artists and Artisans: The ARoS exhibition showcased emerging artists and support local craftsmanship. African curators can:
    • Artist Development Programmes: Offer mentorship and training programmes to support emerging African artists.
    • Collaboration with Artisans: Partner with local artisans to create unique exhibition elements or merchandise.
    • Engaging Children and elderly people: Partner with organizations and schools that can curate workshops within the exhibition to include kids activities and events for the elderly.
  8. Document and Archive Exhibitions: The ARoS exhibition had a strong emphasis on documentation and archiving. African curators can:
    • Digital Archives: Create digital archives of exhibitions, including photographs, videos, and social media documentation.
    • Oral Histories: Interview artists and curators to capture the stories and insights behind the exhibition to share during the program and after.

Incorporating these tips can support African curators and producers in creating dynamic, engaging, and culturally relevant art exhibitions that resonate with both local and international audiences.
Blog Title: Tips and Tricks to Keep Your Exhibition Alive

Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) affects more than 230 million girls and women worldwide, leaving lifelong physical and emotional scars. Despite being illegal in Kenya, the practice continues underground, putting countless young lives at risk. The act is often carried out in secret at home, or in clinics, emphasizing the importance of healthcare professionals having the knowledge and skills to identify, treat, and advocate against this harmful practice. But change is happening, one workshop at a time.

At the forefront of this fight is the Africa Coordinating Centre for Abandonment of Female Genital Mutilation (ACCAF), an organisation based at the University of Nairobi and dedicated to eradicating FGM. In collaboration with the Aga Khan University School of Nursing and Midwifery, East Africa (SONAM EA), ACCAF recently held a transformative one-day workshop for second-year direct-entry nursing students. Led by Dr Joyce Jebet, a faculty member in the midwifery department at SONAM EA and a key member of ACCAF, the workshop aimed to sensitize future healthcare professionals on FGM prevention and response.

The workshop provided a deep dive into the multifaced issue of FGM, including its epidemiology and underlying drivers. Participants delved into the complex management of both immediate and long-term complications, from physical to psychological impacts. Crucial surgical interventions, including de-infibulation and other forms of care for survivors were thoroughly examined. 

Furthermore, the workshop equipped attendees with essential counselling and communication strategies tailored for survivor support, while also grounding them in the legal and human rights framework that seeks to eradicate FGM. A critical component focused on advocacy against the alarming trend of medicalization, highlighting the urgent need to counter this dangerous practice. 

It wasn't just a lecture; it was a dynamic space for learning and dialogue. Students actively participated, asking thoughtful questions and sharing their own insights. For many, it was an eye-opening experience that deepened their understanding of FGM and its far-reaching consequences. 

Armed with this knowledge, these future nurses and midwives are now better prepared to provide compassionate care to FGM survivors, advocate for prevention in their communities, and challenge the medicalization of FGM. During their clinical placements, they can become ambassadors of change, creating a ripple effect that could save countless lives. 

At SONAM EA, we take pride in exposing our nursing students to the right knowledge and skills early in their education. Workshops like this are a cornerstone of preparing them for the realities of the clinical setting and equipping them to make a meaningful impact in their communities.
Blog Title: Empowering Change
Summary: How a Workshop is Equipping Nursing students to Combat FGM

In Dar es Salaam, a reproductive health crisis persists, particularly among adolescents in underserved communities. AKU’s School of Nursing and Midwifery, East Africa (SONAM EA) students in Tanzania, as part of their community midwifery course, witnessed these challenges firsthand during home visits. They observed young mothers lacking guidance, male hesitancy in antenatal care, and widespread knowledge gaps.

Determined to make a difference, the students, together with the BSc Nursing – Direct Entry class and under the guidance of faculty members Dr Eunice Siaity, Lucy Kisaka, and Dr Stewart Mbelwa, organized a two-day community outreach initiative on February 27 and 28, 2025. 

They visited Saranga Street in Ubungo Municipal and Minondo Street in Kigamboni Municipal, which are known to have rampant reproductive health challenges. Their mission: to provide health care and promote lasting change.

SONAM students led health education sessions, using engaging role plays and demonstrations to break the silence around topics often whispered about but rarely understood. One such session left a lasting impact on a mother of three from Minondo.

“I used to delay my antenatal care visits, thinking it wasn’t urgent until much later in my pregnancy,” she admitted after watching a skit on the risks of late clinic visits. “Now, I understand the dangers and the importance of starting early. From now on, I will follow what I’ve learned and make sure I attend all my appointments.”

A key thing students hoped to address during this community visit was the breakdown of deep-seated cultural barriers, particularly concerning male involvement in reproductive health. A local street chairman candidly admitted the struggles men face in participating in antenatal care. “In our community, a man going with his wife to the clinic is seen as strange. Carrying her bag? Sitting beside her as she speaks with a midwife? People will laugh,” he said with a chuckle. 

As the days unfolded, it became evident that such community visits are much more than a learning experience. Lucy Kisaka, a faculty member at SONAM and a co-facilitator of the Community Midwifery Course, found herself deeply moved by the experience.

“Guiding and supervising the students in the community was a learning process for me as well,” she reflected. “Midwifery in a community setting is more than just clinical skills, it’s about understanding social dynamics, breaking cultural barriers, and fostering trust.”

For the students, the experience was eye-opening. One BScM student, who attended as an invited guest, left with a newfound sense of purpose. “This experience has shown me the gaps that exist in reproductive health access,” she said. “As I prepare for my own community placement next year, I feel more prepared to advocate for better awareness and accessibility.”

By the end of the community outreach, many members within these communities had received the care they sought, and countless conversations had been sparked. This was a powerful testament of AKU SONAM students, stepping beyond the classroom and textbooks and immersing themselves in the realities of the communities they aspire to serve throughout their nursing journey.
Blog Title: Midwifery Students Bring Hope to Underserved Communities

Authors: Ayesha Mansoor and Azra Naseem


When ChatGPT launched in November 2022, it sparked a ton of discussion about how it 

would impact teaching and learning, students' cognitive skills, creativity and originality of work. Some even wondered if teachers would be replaced with LLMs in the near future. Faculty members were pretty worried, students were using the tools a lot, and faculty developers weren't sure what their new roles would be (Chuhao et al., 2024). However, in all this debate, one thing was clear: teaching and learning will go through significant changes and faculty must be prepared to adapt. 


We talked with two undergraduate medical faculty members at Aga Khan University (AKU) to understand how they use GenAI in their teaching and learning and what medical faculty can do to improve their teaching practices. For this discussion, we invited Prof. Simiat Elias, Founding Chair of the Biomedical Sciences Department at Aga Khan University in Nairobi, Kenya and Dr Sadia Fatima, Associate Professor Department of Biomedical and Biological Sciences Department and Chair of the Haile T. Debas Teacher’s Academy. The discussion was moderated by Azra Naseem, Director Blended and Digital Learning, Network of Quality, Teaching and Learning and Senior Instructor Institute for Educational Development. 

How are faculty using GenAI?

Recognising the need to adopt digital technologies to improve student learning and pedagogies, Aga Khan University encourages the use of GenAI tools in teaching, learning, research and administrative processes. 

 

Both Dr Sadia and Dr Simiat mentioned that they are using GenAI in a number of ways to facilitate their teaching and incorporate the use of GenAI tools in student learning. Some of the most common tools they used were ChatGPT, Gemini, Gamma, DALL.E and Copilot, which helped them save time on tasks that otherwise took hours to do. 


Some of the examples of how they are using GenAI tools are: 

  • Creating slides

  • Making illustrations

  • Generating questions for a quiz 

  • Summarizing information

  • Generating references 

  • Refining lesson plans 

  • Creating case studies

  • Ideas for formative assessment 


They also mentioned that they tasked students to create a learning resource using ChatGPT 3.0 and then compare it to the resources given by her. This class discussion, which took place in 2023, resulted in students realising that the faculty resource was more thorough and useful. However, since then, ChatGPT and other such LLMs have gone through significant upgrades and are now better equipped and more knowledgeable than when they were initially launched. 


Currently, the faculty is also supporting students in using GenAI tools to search literature, analyse data and create infographics and short videos to summarise lengthy resources that are difficult and boring to read each time. 

How are students using GenAI tools? 

Students are using GenAI for a variety of things, and most are using it multiple times a day. Some of the most common ways are concept explanation, exam preparation, summarization, visualisation of complex concepts, creating diagrams, etc. 


However, students also found that GenAI tends to hallucinate a lot of information.

Changes to Pedagogy and Assessment 

Monologues are not the way to go!


Faculty quickly realised that if their assessments could be easily done by ChatGPT and other GenAI tools, then what would be the purpose of assessment? 


Recognising this, Dr Sadia used an ingenious hack - asking ChatGPT! She used the tool to identify different assessment strategies that she could use, which cannot be hacked using a GenAI tool. This included Pecha Kucha, a flipped classroom approach, class discussions and presentations. Similarly, Dr Simiat focused on students being able to critically connect different concepts together, explain them and role-play in class. Her assessments moved from traditional paper writing to critical analysis and critique. 


But that wasn’t enough. They also wanted to build their students' critical AI literacy through their courses, so they started creating activities that involved using GenAI tools for class discussions, critiques and debates. They decided that teachers can no longer be the “Sages on the stage” and that it's important to responsibly use GenAI tools to improve class engagement. 


They have replaced traditional lectures with class discussions and student-led learning. 

Challenges of using GenAI tools 

Trusting AI blindly! 


The first challenge was, of course, that students can easily access information, so the faculty must rethink their role as facilitators and revise their pedagogy and assessment. 

Some of the most common challenges that the faculty encountered were the inaccurate information given by GenAI tools and the lengthy responses. However, improved prompting and continuous learning helped them get better at using the tools and understanding their limitations. 


However, many students continue to over-rely on the information given by these tools and do not verify its accuracy. When most students use these tools to answer questions, the entire class’s responses come out very similar. Some students also input confidential data into the GenAI tools. Faculty also tend to overuse the tools especially when they generate assessment questions using these tools. While it's okay to brainstorm questions and ideas for questions directly, using the questions it generates in assignments poses a risk—others may have access to the same questions or may already be prepared for them. 


To address this, awareness raising has to be done amongst both faculty and students. For instance, Dr Sadia spoke to her students, highlighting that they may pass the exam using GenAI, but when they encounter an actual patient and have to do differential diagnosis and recommend tests and treatment, they will struggle because their concepts are not as clear. 

Can GenAI use negatively affect the development of creativity and problem-solving skills? 

Not at all! Students are actually thinking in new and innovative ways. 


GenAI is not affecting students' creativity but, in fact, helping them work together. Through group activities, students are able to build soft skills like better communication, leadership, critical thinking and peer learning. It helps by doing the mundane tasks while letting you focus on the creative and critical thinking aspects. For instance, in Dr Simiat’s class, she has made sure that students must interact with GenAI tools and contextualise responses so the answers can’t be directly copy-pasted. Similarly, students also use the speech feature to have conversations with GenAI to understand concepts in a language that they understand best. 

Competencies needed by faculty and students 

Practise lifelong learning 


This technology is here to stay and disrupt the way we teach and learn, so it’s important to build faculty capacity and student literacy in these areas: 

  • Basics of AI and GenAI 

  • Responsible and ethical use of GenAI (privacy, data protection, ownership, etc.)

  • Change in traditional assessments and student learning outcomes

  • Critical appraisal and analysis of information 


Faculty are actively using, learning, and experimenting with these technologies, recognizing the importance of adapting pedagogy and assessments to remain effective and relevant in teaching students in this era. While generic GenAI tools like ChatGPT and DeepSeek should not be used for grading or providing direct feedback to students due to their lack of transparency in the use of user data, they can still be a valuable tool in designing assessments that promote critical thinking.

Although many countries have access to the latest encrypted AI models through licensed, paid versions, there is also the possibility of creating and training your own LLM using open-source APIs, which can be tailored to your students' needs and will be completely encrypted and controlled.

Authors: Azra Naseem and Ayesha Mansoor, with assistance from ChatGPT.


The first EdTech Lounge of 2023, led by Azra Naseem Director Blended Digital Learning, Aga Khan University, elicited a range of emotions from 100+ participants, excitement, fear, thoughtfulness, and even intimidation. The session, organised by the Network of Quality Teaching and Learning (QTL_net)​, AKU, aimed to explore the potential impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on academics, students, and educational institutions.

While AI presents novel possibilities for educational development, teaching, and learning, it also brings forth challenges, such as disruptions to traditional assessment methods and plagiarism, hence raising questions about academic integrity. In a bid to address these issues, participants from Universities across Pakistan, Kyrgyzstan, Kenya, UAE, Canada, UK, USA, Uganda, India and Tanzania joined the session and actively engaged in a conversation to address complex questions around the topic.

During the session, Ms. Naseem introduced participants to various OpenAI tools, including DALL-E, an AI system that creates images from textual descriptions using deep learning techniques, and ChatGPT, a language model based on AI technology that can generate human-like responses to a wide range of text-based queries. It will be exceedingly challenging to limit student access to AI as it continues to develop and integrate with the tools we commonly use, such as MS Word or TEAMS. Therefore, faculty needs to work with these tools and understand how AI might benefit students in the learning process while ensuring academic integrity. She highlighted that the question is no longer whether we should use AI or not but rather how to leverage it effectively and equip students with the necessary competencies for navigating complex and ever-evolving times. The digital gap will make it increasingly difficult for students and graduates to compete in the real world, thus it is crucial for institutions like AKU to recognise any potential inequalities that might exist between AI-haves and AI-have-nots.

A Padlet wall was made available during the session to facilitate conversation around five questions. An overview of comments made by attendees on the Zoom Chat and Padlet Wall is shown below:

What possibilities do AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) offer for your teaching or course?

There was an agreement that AI can serve as a vital academic tool by providing teachers with ease in developing course plans, assessment tools, and grading rubrics while improving student engagement and critical thinking. One of the participant’s noted that "ChatGPT is everyone's best friend" since it streamlines tedious and time-consuming tasks, making them more efficient and organised. Few participants also shared via comments on Zoom how using ChatGPT was helping them in making presentations for the class as well as accomplishing other tasks.

What concerns you most about using AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) in your course or teaching?

When participants were asked about their concerns with using this emerging technology in courses, responses varied from concerns over the digital divide to inhibiting human creativity and critical thinking. The most significant worry, however, centered around plagiarism in assessments like drafting papers, attempting quizzes, and assignments that couldn't be captured by plagiarism-checking software like Turnitin. Additionally, it was observed that ChatGPT performs independent of religious, cultural, gender, and social contexts, making it unreliable for every situation. One participant noted, "It may interfere with creativity and critical thinking skills. We may end up with students who know a lot of theory or content but cannot apply that knowledge to situations."


How do we (faculty) prepare for AI-based teaching?

ChatGPT can function as a free-of-cost teaching assistant that is just a click away. Multiple faculty members noted that instead of being intimidated by fast-changing technology, faculty should embrace AI and work towards integrating it into the curriculum. Moreover, ChatGPT can provide a framework for designing curriculum, instructional material, or anything that can be further enhanced and contextualised. One respondent also joked about how instructors could finally have a “teaching assistant” without putting in any effort.​

How do we prepare our students for an AI-based world?

Respondents agreed that Gen-Z students and the upcoming generations are better equipped to use technology. Hence, primary education should branch out from the traditional curriculum and modes of teaching and instead focus on building critical skills and empowering students to use AI like ChatGPT and contribute to and debate the ethical limitations and use of such technology. A participant noted in the Zoom Chat that the quality of the output depends on the quality of the query, which requires careful consideration. As a result, educators should adjust their teaching approaches in response to the fact that AI is no longer merely a science fiction concept, but a tangible reality.

What (research) questions are worth exploring?

Below is a list of research themes the participants were interested in exploring.

  • Changing the nature of assessment as we incorporate AI in T-L and curriculum development.
  • How does the use of AI affect the course learning outcomes?
  • What are the ethical implications of using AI-based systems in various applications, such as customer service, mental health counselling and education? This can involve examining issues such as privacy, consent and the potential impact of AI-generated responses on human behaviour.
  • What are the new competencies and readiness requirements for adopting AI in teaching and learning?
  • What are the ethical and academic integrity requirements for using AI-based teaching and learning approaches?

The session concluded by acknowledging that using AI in courses has positive and negative implications. AI can enhance the learning experience by personalising education, automating administrative tasks, and providing real-time feedback to students. AI-powered learning tools can also help students with special needs and those with difficulty learning in a traditional classroom setting. Additionally, AI can improve the efficiency of assessment, freeing up teachers to focus on more complex tasks like providing feedback during one-on-one interactions with students. However, there are also concerns that overreliance on AI could lead to a lack of creativity and critical thinking skills among students. Moreover, the use of AI may lead to job displacement for teachers and raise ethical concerns around data privacy, algorithmic bias, and the use of AI in decision-making. Therefore, it is crucial to consider the implications of AI in classrooms carefully and ensure that it is used responsibly and ethically. It was also mutually agreed that a special interest group can be formed with academics to research, investigate, and share findings that can aid in incorporating AI in teaching and learning especially in the global south. As an immediate way forward, more awareness-raising sessions are needed for faculty, staff and students to understand the use of AI tools in teaching and learning.

This week comes another collaboration between Aga Khan University, Institute for Educational Development and Ziauddin University of Language, Arts, and Culture as we turn our attention to a critical yet often overlooked issue: mental health stigma in Pakistan. The blog explores how cultural silence, misconceptions, and societal pressures have made mental health a taboo topic across communities. Rooted in deep-seated beliefs and social norms, the stigma prevents individuals from acknowledging mental health struggles, seeking timely help, or even discussing their emotional well-being.

Stigma Begins Within

The first battle often begins in the mind of the individual. At the intrapersonal level, people internalize negative beliefs about their condition. Many feel shame, fear judgment, or attribute their symptoms to supernatural causes such as black magic or the evil eye (Choudhry et al., 2018). This cultural narrative delays intervention and deters individuals from seeking professional help. As one patient in a Peshawar psychiatric unit shared, “I just tell everyone that I have a heart problem when someone asks” (Khan & Irfan, 2023, p. 1413). The emotional isolation and self-stigma further erode their well-being. In many households, mental illness is not seen as a medical condition; it’s seen as a moral weakness or personality flaw. As a result, emotional vulnerability is discouraged, and those who struggle are often urged to "toughen up" or "pray more." This lack of open conversation leads to underdiagnosis, untreated trauma, and prolonged suffering.

The Gendered Face of Stigma

Mental health stigma is particularly harsh for women. Cultural expectations dictate that women should be emotionally resilient, sacrificial, and selfless. They are often discouraged from voicing psychological distress, especially if it could reflect poorly on family honour. A patient recalled, "My traumatic childhood was considered a self-created drama until things got worse" (Talat et al., 2022, p. 563). Financial dependence, restricted mobility, and a lack of decision-making power only compound these barriers (Khan & Irfan, 2023; Nisar et al., 2019).
During and after pregnancy, the silence deepens. Husbands may focus solely on financial provision, overlooking emotional care, while mothers are expected to prioritise their baby’s health over their own (Shafiq, 2024; McCauley et al., 2020). These pressures make postpartum depression and anxiety not only common but also tragically normalised.

Spiritual Healing vs. Professional Help

Treatment-seeking behaviour in Pakistan often follows a familiar path: families turn first to local physicians, traditional healers, or religious figures such as Pirs and Maulvis. Psychiatric consultation becomes the last resort, only considered when spiritual methods fail or when symptoms escalate into risky behaviour (Shah et al., 2019). As one father insisted, “My daughter is just suffering from evil eye... she will be fine with the grace of God and my spiritual healer” (Javed et al., 2020, p. 563). While faith can be a source of comfort, relying exclusively on it delays timely intervention and reinforces misinformation.

The Role of Education and Institutions

Educational institutions, schools, colleges, and universities hold immense potential to dismantle the mental health stigma in Pakistan. These spaces are not just for academic instruction but also for shaping mindsets and social values. By introducing age-appropriate discussions on mental health in curricula, institutions can nurture emotional literacy from an early age. Teachers can be trained to recognise signs of distress and refer students for appropriate support. Schools can also host awareness campaigns, workshops, and seminars involving students, parents, and staff to demystify mental health and promote empathy. Mental health stigma in Pakistan thrives on silence, misunderstanding, and fear. But we can rewrite the story, especially within the education sector.
