It has been a month since we returned home, yet the memories of Tanzania remain as vivid as the wide skies above the savannah. That place was more than a destination; it gave us room to learn, to reflect, and most importantly, to draw inspiration. And when I think back, one image always rises above the rest: the “people who read the clouds.”

In today’s world of accelerating climate change, people respond differently. Some seek safety in distant cities, leaving behind vulnerable homelands. Even those who work for their communities often do so from afar, keeping themselves away from the everyday hardships of rural life. It is rare to meet someone who not only returns but chooses to live fully in the very place others escape from.

During our internship at AKU’s Arusha Climate and Environmental Research Centre (AKU-ACER), we had the privilege of meeting such a person: Alais Morindat, a Maasai pastoralist, community leader, and visionary. He describes his people as “those who read the cloud,” a reference to their ancestral gift of interpreting skies and rainfall to make vital decisions. Meeting him in Monduli, a Maasai village about a50-minute drive from AKU-ACER, among the open grasslands, reshaped our idea of what it means to serve one’s people.

The Maasai, semi-nomadic pastoralists of East Africa, have for centuries lived in harmony with their cattle, the land, and the savannah. Cattle are their lifeblood: wealth, food, culture, and spirituality. Yet climate change has unsettled this delicate rhythm. Erratic rains, longer droughts, and shrinking pastures have put livestock and livelihoods at risk. Many young people migrate to cities, searching for different futures. Alais, however, walked a different path.

After studying abroad in Ireland and being exposed to modern comforts, he could have stayed. But he returned home. He built a modern house, yes, but he never abandoned his pastoralist identity. Instead, he created a life that blends the two worlds: modern innovations and Maasai traditions, side by side.

One of Alais’s most striking contributions has been in livestock feeding. His land sustains large herds of cattle, goats, and sheep that depend on consistent forage even as the climate grows harsher. To address this, he introduced resilient grasses, with support from AKU-ACER, including Bana grass, a high-nutrient variety that stays green year-round and requires planting only once. This ensures that even during long dry seasons, animals have enough to feed on. He also practices controlled grazing, protecting young grass until it matures, allowing the land to recover and hold water longer.

But Alais did not stop there. On his farm, he has established sustainable plantations growing a variety of grass and fodder trees that enrich the soil while providing food for livestock. These plantations are carefully managed so that the land is not depleted but continuously renewed. Walking through his homestead, one sees a landscape that reflects both careful planning and deep respect for the earth.

Perhaps what is most inspiring is how seamlessly Alais blends modern life with pastoralist traditions. His house may have the comforts of the present day, but right outside, cattle still graze, children learn the ways of herding, and elders gather to share stories. He embodies the idea that modernity does not have to erase tradition; rather, the two can strengthen each other. He is a great example that the modern scientific world and traditional cultural life can go hand in hand.

Through indigenous wisdom and practical innovation, Alais is tackling soil erosion, a problem many experts consider unsolvable in drylands. Using local resources, simple barriers, and Maasai techniques, he has slowed runoff, regenerated degraded soils, and brought life back to barren patches. Today, his land is dotted with lush green, where only dust and erosion scars remain.

Alais is more than a climate leader. He is a storyteller, a bridge between past and present, and a living example of what it means to return and give back. His life teaches us that progress is not about abandoning roots, but about carrying them forward, enriching them with new knowledge and passing them on to future generations.

In the vast savannah of Tanzania, we discovered that resilience is not written only in textbooks or policies, but in the clouds, the land, and the lives of people like Alais Morindat, those who choose to stay, rebuild, and inspire hope.

On a hot afternoon in an urban informal settlement in Nairobi, we meet Joyce, not her real name, a Community Health Promoter (CHP) who narrates the difficult circumstances in which she performs her tasks.

As a CHP, she has a clear mission: check in on families, share health information, and guide them on where to seek care when needed. However, often, what awaits her is not a warm welcome.

“In some households, people are angry or stressed and take it out on me. They do not want to talk, and sometimes they are very rude.” she says.

For Joyce, who supports 100 households including her own, the emotional toll is heavy. A single bad encounter can put her in a sour mood the entire day.

“When one of the household members shouts at me, I leave feeling angry. I carry that weight home, and unfortunately, my family feels it too.”

At home, small inconveniences often trigger an overreaction.

 “When my child misbehaves, all the bottled-up anger from the day comes out and I punish her more harshly than I should. It is not fair to her,” she adds.

A new beginning

One day, her supervisor informed her and her colleagues of a mental well-being and resilience training programme offered by the Aga Khan University Institute for Human Development (IHD) with support from the Johnson & Johnson Foundation.

The programme comprised of two interventions – a mental health literacy programme and the World Health Organization (WHO) developed Self Help Plus (SH+) course. 

The mental health literacy programme incorporated modules to raise mental health awareness, challenge stigma, promote early help-seeking behaviour and encourage positive coping strategies. 

The SH+ course is a 5-session stress management course for adults who experience stressful conditions. It has been shown to reduce psychological distress and prevent the onset of mental disorders.

For the first time, CHPs like her, often the first point of contact for health issues in the community, were being offered tools to care for their own mental well-being. 

“I signed up immediately,” Joyce says, her eyes gleaming with joy. “We always help others, but no one ever asks about our mental health. This was our chance to get the support we needed.”

Through the training, Joyce learnt practical ways to manage stress, ease tense situations, and handle her emotions.

“I learnt how to react to people when they are angry or in a bad mood. Now, when someone seems stressed or upset, I probe further and try to find out what is wrong. It has completely changed how I relate to households.”

Families who once shut her out now welcome her visits. Conversations flow easily, her work feels more fulfilling, and she reaches more people.

 At home, the transformation was just as powerful.

“I no longer shout when I am upset. I take time to talk to my child and show her love. Our home feels peaceful now and my child talks to me openly because she knows I will listen.”

Championing mental health in the community

The training not only changed Joyce’s personal life but also shifted how she views mental health in her community.
“Before, I feared people with mental health disorders. I avoided them,” she admits. “But now I know they need help, not isolation.”

Armed with new knowledge, Joyce and her fellow CHPs are now sensitising the community about mental health. They are encouraging people to support rather than shun those in distress.

“Sometimes you find that a person is not suffering from a mental illness but rather the person is stressed. People need someone to talk to, someone who understands,” she adds.

Through the programme, over 600 healthcare workers in Nairobi County including community health promoters, nurses, clinical officers, medical officers, laboratory and pharmacy personnel have been trained to better care for their own mental well-being and guide others to seek help when needed.
Blog Title: Delivered from the shackles of stress
Summary: IHD programme champions mental well-being among community health promoters

Blog Detail:
Mercy, not her real name, a Nurse in-charge and Director at a Medical Centre in Nairobi, recalls the frustration she would feel while on duty.

“As I went about my supervisory duties, I would follow up with patients after their sessions to understand if they received appropriate care and guidance. Sometimes I would discover that the patients were not well taken care of, despite the team having all the information they needed. It was upsetting.”

Situations such as these would aggravate Mercy. At times, she admits, she felt like lashing out at her staff, wondering why they ignored clear instructions that could improve patients’ health outcomes.

A new way of leading

The turning point for Mercy came after she and her colleagues enrolled in the Mental Well-being and Resilience Programme offered by the Aga Khan University Institute for Human Development. The programme, supported by the Johnson & Johnson Foundation, was designed to help health care workers improve their mental well-being.

One incident stands out clearly in Mercy’s memory. As she spoke to mothers visiting the clinic, she realised that they were not receiving all the necessary reproductive health information. 

“I reached out to the nurse responsible and asked her to counsel the mothers before they left the clinic,” Mercy says. A few days later, I found out it was still not happening. “Before the training, I might have confronted her angrily. However, this time, I took some time to calm down and then walked over to her station to talk to her.’’
The nurse explained that the task was new to her routine, so she sometimes forgot to incorporate it but promised to improve.

Mercy realised that by staying calm and seeking to understand first, she could resolve problems without creating tension.  

“My response to difficult situations has changed,” she says. “Now I take time to analyse the problem, manage my emotions, and act in a way that actually helps.”

Her new leadership style, coupled with the mental health literacy training that her staff went through, led to a positive transformation in the health centre.

“The team became more cooperative, more open, and more motivated to do things right,” Mercy adds.

Personal growth

The benefits of the training extended far beyond her workplace. 

Before, Mercy often harboured stress which affected her personal relationships. “I would constantly worry about things that were out of my control. As a result, I became moody and sometimes this led to conflicts with my family.”

Through the training, Mercy learned practical tools for coping with anxiety and managing her emotions.

“I now acknowledge when I am feeling overwhelmed and give myself time to cool down,” she explains. “I focus on the things I can change instead of worrying about what I cannot.”

This mindset shift has brought more peace into her personal life. “I prioritise positive actions for my family during difficult times,” Mercy says. 

For Mercy, the Mental Health Literacy training was not just about learning new skills. It was about transforming how she sees herself, her work and the people around her.

Mercy is among the 600 health care workers who went through the transformative training that took place over an eight-week period in various health facilities in Nairobi.
Blog Title: From Frustration to Transformation
Summary: A Nurse’s Journey to Mental Well-Being

Blog Detail:
At the Sixth Conference on Land Policy in Africa (CLPA), the call was clear: Africa must break free from colonial land systems and boldly reimagine its relationship with land. From Supreme Court justices to ministers and scholars, speakers insisted on moving beyond lamentation toward liberation. The call was not simply to decolonize land laws, but to transform them – creatively, unapologetically, and with the future in mind.

This urgent shift is intensified by the climate crisis, where outdated and exclusionary land systems only deepen vulnerabilities. African institutions, especially universities, must redesign curricula and research agendas to integrate climate literacy across all disciplines, ensuring graduates are equipped to navigate climate, justice, and sustainability.

Why This Moment Matters

The conference theme “Land Governance, Justice and Reparations for Africans and Descendants of People of the African Diaspora” drew on a painful yet necessary truth that African land and people for centuries been targeted by other nations for raw materials and labour. The legacies of enslavement, colonial plunder, and economic extraction remain deeply embedded in current land systems. Understanding these histories is not optional—it is foundational, because in a changing climate, this weight becomes heavier, demanding just and innovative land governance.

Voices from the Plenary and Technical Sessions

The United Nations Under-Secretary-General and Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA), Mr Claver Gatete, urged African countries to strengthen land administration systems and ensure land is productively used. He challenged the longstanding dependence on exporting raw materials, and emphasized harnessing diaspora capital and technology for resilience.

Ambassador Amr Aljowaily of the African Union Commission spoke of land as a mirror reflecting Africa’s broader struggles—identity, ownership, justice, and survival. He stressed that “the African decade of justice must be grounded in truth,” arguing that revisiting colonial history is key to understanding inequitable systems and crafting meaningful reforms. The challenge, he stated, is to translate reparative justice into forward-looking institutional reform.

Kenyan artist Scar of ‘Scar Poetry,’ used her powerful performance to remind delegates that justice and reparation are not abstract ideas—they are emotional, spiritual, and historical necessities. As one line declared, “We have been here before. But this time, may we stay long enough for the land to heal.”

South Africa’s Minister of Land Reform emphasized that land remains the foundation of food security, social stability, and cultural identity. He called for stronger collaboration between government, universities, and research institutions. “We need new finance models and better policy research,” he urged.

Justice Smokin Wanjala of Kenya’s Supreme Court delivered a sharp critique of Africa’s inherited land systems, describing three colonial harms: the loss of land rights, displacement and identity loss, and the destruction of African land tenure systems. “Colonialism’s objective was to plunder—often by force,” he said. He reminded us that while African liberation movements sought to restore land and dignity, many post-colonial regimes ironically dismissed customary tenure as “backward”, reproducing colonial attitudes. His was warning was to avoid “perpetuating old continuities.”

Dr Dozwa from Zimbabwe outlined her country’s deliberate move to break from colonial land structures, after the “willing buyer, willing seller” model failed. Fast-track land reform redistributing land and, she stated, has led to self-sufficiency in key crops. Her firm conclusion: “Colonial continuity is a choice of leadership.”

Technical sessions highlighted chronic underinvestment in land governance. Speakers noted that technology, such as digital land data and AI, offers opportunity but risks enabling elite capture if safeguards are absent.

Onyekachi Wambu reminded the audience that Africa has thousands of years of experience solving its own problems. Reclaiming trust in African institutions, leadership, and knowledge systems is therefore central to breaking colonial continuities.

Toward Liberated Land and Liberated Futures

The CLPA conversations made one truth undeniable: Africa’s land question is not technical—it is historical, political, cultural, economic, and spiritual. Land reform must reclaim identity, restore dignity, and prepare societies for climate-driven futures. It must be inclusive, innovative, and grounded in justice.

Liberating land means liberating the systems, ideas, and people tied to it.

It means speaking boldly, without apology.

It means trusting African solutions and African futures.
Blog Title: From Decolonizing to Liberating Land in Africa’s Changing Climate

On International Day of Education, it is worth asking a simple question. Who shapes learning in our universities?

At Aga Khan University, the answer is clear. Our students do.

Across our campuses in Pakistan, Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania, students are leading societies, creating peer learning spaces, organising wellness initiatives, and applying academic knowledge to real-world challenges. In doing so, they are influencing how learning is experienced beyond the classroom.

Student-led clubs and societies remain among the most effective learning environments at AKU. New societies introduced in 2025, alongside established groups, have strengthened leadership, collaboration, and practical skills development. Through health awareness initiatives, academic forums, creative platforms, and community engagement, students are translating theory into practice and learning through responsibility.

This leadership is equally visible in peer learning and wellbeing initiatives. Mentorship programmes, Stress Awareness Week, and Suicide Prevention Day activities were shaped by strong student involvement, reinforcing the idea that academic success is closely linked to care, connection, and support. Students are also contributing to knowledge creation through symposiums, quiz-based learning activities, and interdisciplinary discussions with faculty. Beyond classrooms, initiatives such as the AKU Sports Olympiad, Rowing Regatta, and Sports Fiestas show how teamwork, leadership, and resilience are developed through experience.

As Vice Provost Students and Head of Student Affairs, I am inspired by how our students engage with education as a shared endeavour. On this International Day of Education, we celebrate their leadership and creativity, and we reaffirm our commitment to learning shaped together across our campuses.

Education is strongest when students are trusted with responsibility. That is the kind of learning environment we must continue to build.​
Blog Title: International Day of Education: Who Shapes Learning?

Volunteerism is embedded in my family's DNA. I grew up witnessing my parents and grandparents serving to build a more just society. My journey with the Aga Khan University (AKU) began in 1988, providing health support during its inauguration. Prior to that, I worked with the Aga Khan Health Board on initiatives ranging from goitre prevention to chronic disease management.

What continues to motivate me is the opportunity to contribute to something larger than myself, supporting the development of people and systems that improve health outcomes, reduce inequities, and help create a knowledge-based society that benefits communities locally, regionally, and globally.

Serving others brings deep fulfilment. My service aligns with AKU's mission to improve quality of life through education and health care. This reflects values I hold dear: pluralism, excellence, and a commitment to long-term capacity-building rather than short-term solutions.

My background in medicine and public health has allowed me to find meaning through the Time and Knowledge Nazrana (TKN), contributing at the intersection of clinical practice, education, and health systems. Over the past decade, I have mentored residents and faculty in health care education and research, particularly in East Africa.

As a mentor, the defining moment is when a mentee excels and surpasses you in achievement. I have seen a student from a small village become a cardiologist serving his community, and others rise to become department chairs. These "ah-ha" moments reinforce the importance of mutual learning. I believe it is better to light one candle than to curse the darkness.

Over 25 years, seeing medical students grow into directors and division chiefs, becoming mentors themselves, has been immensely rewarding. Volunteering has enriched me by broadening my perspective and deepening my cultural humility.

Volunteering requires emotional investment and time, but what one receives in return is far greater: a profound sense of connection and enduring relationships. Plus, experiencing other cultures has made this journey fun.

Looking ahead, there is tremendous potential for TKN to expand interdisciplinary education and research capacity. To future volunteers, my advice is simple: approach this work with humility and patience. Strive to see the world through the eyes of those you serve; often, you will learn far more than you ever imagined.
Blog Title: The DNA of Service: Mentorship, Growth, and the Spirit of Volunteerism

Blog Detail:
What if education didn't stop at teaching concepts, but truly prepared learners for real-life decisions, pressure, and responsibility before they ever faced a patient?

That question sits at the heart of simulation-based education, an approach that is transforming how healthcare professionals are prepared for practice across the world, and increasingly, right here in Pakistan.

A Brief History

Throughout the ages, physicians and surgeons have learnt their skills on real patients, a practice that continues to this day. While this is essential for skill development, it exposes the patient to possible medical errors. This is where simulation-based education comes in.

Early forms of simulation emerged in aviation and the military, where safe practice in high-risk environments was essential. Healthcare soon followed, from simple anatomical models to later, high-fidelity manikins, standardised patients, and digital and immersive technologies.

Globally, simulation gained momentum as patient safety became a central concern. At AKU, simulation has evolved into a strategic educational tool - integrated across curricula and professional development through the Centre for Innovation in Medical Education (CIME), now present in four countries where AKU operates: Pakistan, Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda.

Why Simulation Matters - Especially in Pakistan

Healthcare education in Pakistan operates within complex realities: high patient loads, limited time for supervision, unequal exposure to clinical cases, and significant pressure on training systems.

Simulation addresses these challenges, allowing students and professionals to:

  • Practise critical skills safely
  • Experience rare or high-risk scenarios
  • Build confidence, teamwork, and clinical reasoning
  • Learn from mistakes without fear or harm
How Simulation-Based Education Works

Simulation is not defined by equipment - it is defined by intention. At its core, it is a structured educational method designed to prepare learners for complexity.

At CIME, simulation-based education includes:

  • Carefully designed clinical scenarios based on real healthcare challenges
  • The use of manikins, task trainers, VR, and simulated patients for practice.
  • Debriefing sessions where reflection and learning are deepened
  • Interprofessional learning that brings together doctors, nurses, and allied health professionals
Common Myths

Despite its proven value, a few misconceptions persist:

  • “Simulation cannot take the place of real patients."
    Simulation is not meant to take the place of real patients. It builds confidence and competence by letting learners make mistakes safely during practice, not on the patient.

  • “Simulation isn't real enough."
    Simulation prepares learners for real practice by focusing on decision-making, communication, leadership, and clinical reasoning - the skills that matter most when lives are at stake.

  • “It's only for students."
    Simulation supports learning across careers, from undergraduate education to senior clinicians refining leadership and crisis-management skills.

  • “It's too expensive for Pakistan."
    Through homegrown, low-cost simulators, AKU has demonstrated that innovation can be local, scalable, and contextually relevant without compromising educational quality.
Why Simulation is Essential for Modern Education

Modern education must prepare learners not only to know, but to act, adapt, and lead. Simulation bridges theory and practice, transforming classrooms into safe environments where confidence is built before clinical responsibility begins.

Looking Ahead

Education that merely teaches is no longer enough. Healthcare education must prepare. And simulation makes that possible.

With AKU's IQRA framework at its core, which emphasises impact, quality, relevance, and access, CIME continues to lead nationally and regionally in healthcare simulation in Pakistan and East Africa, preparing learners not just for examinations, but for the real-world challenges they will face - and the lives they will serve.
Blog Title: Education that Prepares, Not Just Teaches: Simulation in Healthcare

Blog Detail:
​This International Day for Women and Girls in Science, the UN calls on us to synergize AI, social science, STEM, and finance to build inclusive futures for women and girls. 

But in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), inclusion is not created by language. It is created by design. 

I am an electrical engineer. In my graduating class, there were 98 boys and 2 girls. Later, as a professional in software and data, I was — more often than not — the only female executive at the table. At global meetings, men have walked up to me and asked if I could get them coffee. 

Not because they knew me. 

But because they assumed. 

These assumptions are not harmless. They are embedded in classrooms, boardrooms, hiring decisions, and research funding. And they start early. 

Women make up only one in three researchers globally, and less than a third of STEM professionals across Africa. In many Sub-Saharan African countries, fewer than 30% of engineering graduates are women. And yet, when girls are given equal access and encouragement, they perform as well as — and often outperform — boys in math and science. 

The problem is not ability. 

It is access. It is expectation. It is power. 

In many LMIC settings, girls are taught — subtly and explicitly — what is “appropriate.” They are conditioned to choose differently long before they understand their own potential. 

The convergence of AI, STEM, finance, and social science is shaping the next generation of opportunity — and we are entering the AI era with a choice to make. 

And here is the uncomfortable truth: 

AI will not correct inequity. 

AI will not democratise opportunity unless we design for it. 

AI will codify the biases of the past - at scale. 

Because if the data doesn’t see women, the system won’t serve women. 

At Aga Khan University, I lead teams building AI systems to improve outcomes for the communities we serve. That means being intentional. It means designing systems that account for women’s realities, health needs, economic roles, and lived experiences — not as edge cases, but as core users. 

“Building inclusive futures is not about charity.” 

It is about widening the architecture of opportunity. 
Fund girls’ education. Promote women into decision-making. Audit the data shaping your systems. 

When we give girls access, encouragement, and representation, we do not lose ground — we expand it. We gain stronger institutions, smarter systems, and more resilient societies. 

So, this International Day for Women and Girls in Science, my question is simple: 

How will you widen the architecture of opportunity?
Blog Title: Designing Inclusive Futures for Women and Girls
